summary: Source decomposition of CN.0's cost model and CN.1's primality and polynomial-factorization content from Shoup's freely distributed Version 2: the RAM machine model under which every running-time claim is to be read; the Miller-Rabin test with the subgroup L_n, the Carmichael obstruction, the replacement set L'_n and the one-sided error bound |L'_n| <= (n-1)/4; the AKS algorithm with the underlying binomial identity in both directions, the bound O(len(n)^5) on the auxiliary modulus r, the running-time bound O(len(n)^{16.5}) and both correctness statements; and the three-phase factorization of polynomials over a finite field with its exact operation counts, including the tightness of the Cantor-Zassenhaus bound. The result-type distinction that CN.1's acceptance condition demands (probable prime versus proven prime) is made explicit. CN.2 through CN.5 are not read, and it is recorded that the roadmap's declared source cannot supply them.

nodes.title: The RAM machine model and the bit-complexity convention used by all running-time statements
nodes.statement: A RAM consists of an unbounded sequence of memory cells m[0], m[1], m[2], ..., each holding an arbitrary integer, together with a program: a finite sequence of instructions of three types. ARITHMETIC instructions have the form gamma <- alpha * beta where * is addition, subtraction, multiplication or integer division (floor), and alpha, beta are of the form c, m[a] or m[m[a]] and gamma of the form m[a] or m[m[a]], with c an integer constant and a a non-negative integer constant. BRANCHING instructions have the form IF alpha REL beta GOTO i with REL one of =, !=, <, >, <=, >=. The HALT instruction stops execution. Execution starts at I_0 and follows branches until HALT. Input and output are assumed to be in memory cells at prescribed locations; no input/output instructions are specified. COST AND SIZE CONVENTIONS (printed pp. 54-55): the running time of a program on an input is the number of instructions executed (1 unit each); the size of an input is the number of memory cells used to represent it; and for a polynomial-time algorithm all numbers stored in memory must be at most a' n^{b'} + c' in absolute value (after t instructions, at most a'(n+t)^{b'} + c' for any algorithm). Large integers are represented as vectors of base-B digits with B a constant power of 2 (Section 3.3). [Added in review: the draft omitted the unit-cost rule and the magnitude restriction on which the model's meaning depends.]
hypotheses: Memory cells may hold arbitrary integers, but the source charges one unit per instruction AND restricts the magnitude of stored numbers polynomially in the input size and running time. It notes that without this restriction some problems could be solved with polynomially many operations on huge numbers that cannot otherwise be solved in polynomial time (reference to Section 3.6). Large integers are digit vectors in a constant base B, so costs quoted in terms of len(n) are RAM step counts under this convention. [Corrected in review: the draft said the unit-cost reading is 'unrealistic' and that the len(n) convention is what gives the statements meaning; the source's model is unit-cost with a magnitude restriction.]
The instruction set is finite and fixed; in particular integer division is a primitive, which matters for the division-with-remainder analysis

The model is idealized: the source states explicitly that high-level algorithm descriptions 'can be routinely translated into the machine-language of an actual computer' and that the formal model exists 'so that our theorems on the running times of algorithms have a precise mathematical meaning'
proofSteps: The source defines the model directly; there is nothing to prove.
The model is instantiated immediately in section 3.3 on basic integer arithmetic, where the cost of each operation is expressed in terms of the number of base-B digits.

Theorem 3.1 illustrates the level of detail at which the source works: the quotient floor(x/y) is determined by the two high-order digits, precisely 'Let x and y be integers such that 0 <= x = x' 2^n + s and 0 < y = y' 2^n for some integers n, s, x', y' with n >= 0 and 0 <= s < 2^n. Then floor(x/y) = floor(x'/y')'.
acceptance: CN.0's acceptance condition asks that conversions commute with ring/field operations and carry equality/embedding proofs. This node supplies only the machine and cost model; the carrier/representation half is NOT supplied by the sections read.

Check that a claimed running time is a RAM running time in the sense of Section 3.2: unit cost per instruction, numbers in memory polynomially bounded, integers as base-B digit vectors, with sizes measured by len(n). Under this convention a RAM step count and a bit-operation count agree up to constant factors (B is a constant). A cost that allows arbitrarily large integers in single cells is outside the model. [Corrected in review: the draft said bit operations and unit-cost steps differ by an unbounded factor in this model, which the magnitude restriction rules out.]
Check that randomness is a separate resource: the model above is deterministic, and probabilistic algorithms are treated in Shoup Chapter 9, which was not read.

sources.locator: Section 3.2 'Machine models and complexity theory', printed pp. 53-55
sources.excerpt: So that our theorems on the running times of algorithms have a precise mathematical meaning, we formally define an 'idealized' computer: the random access machine or RAM. A RAM consists of an unbounded sequence of memory cells m[0], m[1], m[2], ..., each of which can store an arbitrary integer, together with a program.
sources.match: The model as defined in the source, which is the semantics under which every running-time statement in the other nodes of this packet is to be read.

nodes.title: Miller-Rabin: the sets L_n and L'_n, Carmichael numbers, and the one-sided error bound 1/4
nodes.statement: Define L_n := {alpha in Z_n^+ : alpha^{n-1} = 1}, a subgroup of Z_n^*. (Theorem 10.1) If n is prime then L_n = Z_n^*; if n is composite and L_n is a PROPER subgroup of Z_n^*, then |L_n| <= (n-1)/2. (Theorem 10.2) Every Carmichael number (an odd composite n with L_n = Z_n^*) has the form n = p_1 ... p_r with the p_i distinct primes, r >= 3, and (p_i - 1) | (n - 1). Writing n - 1 = t 2^h with t odd, the Miller-Rabin test uses instead L'_n := {alpha in Z_n^+ : alpha^{t 2^h} = 1 and alpha^{t 2^{j+1}} = 1 implies alpha^{t 2^j} = +-1 for j = 0,...,h-1}; equivalently alpha^t = 1, or the entry of alpha^t, alpha^{2t}, ..., alpha^{t 2^h} immediately before the first 1 is -1. (Theorem 10.3) If n is prime then L'_n = Z_n^*; if n is composite then |L'_n| <= (n-1)/4. Membership in L_n can be tested in time O(len(n)^3) by repeated squaring.
hypotheses: n is the odd integer being tested; the bound (n-1)/4 in Theorem 10.3 holds for EVERY odd composite n, with no Carmichael exception -- that is the whole point of replacing L_n by L'_n
Theorem 10.1's second clause needs the hypothesis that L_n is a PROPER subgroup; without it the bound is false, and Carmichael numbers are exactly the counterexamples
The error is ONE-SIDED: a prime input is always accepted, so a 'composite' answer is certain while a 'prime' answer is probabilistic
The analysis of |L'_n| uses the decomposition n = prod p_i^{e_i}, the cyclic structure of each Z_{p_i^{e_i}}^*, and g := min{h, h_1, ..., h_r} where phi(p_i^{e_i}) = t_i 2^{h_i}
proofSteps: Theorem 10.1: L_n is the kernel of the (n-1)-power map on Z_n^*, hence a subgroup; if n is prime, |Z_n^*| = n-1 and Lagrange gives L_n = Z_n^*; if L_n is proper then |Z_n^*| = t |L_n| with t > 1, so |L_n| <= |Z_n^*|/2 <= (n-1)/2.

Theorem 10.3 (printed pp. 309-310) has three cases. Case 1 (n prime): alpha^{n-1} = 1, and the only elements of order dividing 2 in the cyclic group Z_n^* are +-1. Case 2 (n = p^e, e > 1): L'_n lies in the kernel K of the (n-1)-power map, |K| = gcd(phi(n), n-1) = p - 1 <= (n-1)/4 (Theorem 6.32). Case 3 (r > 1 distinct primes): every alpha in L'_n satisfies alpha^{t 2^g} = 1 with g = min{h, h_1, ..., h_r}, by a minimal-counterexample argument contradicting that the order of alpha_i^t divides |Z_{p_i^{e_i}}^*| (Theorem 6.37). Hence L'_n is contained in rho_{g-1}^{-1}({+-1}), and |L'_n| <= 2 |Ker rho_{g-1}| (10.1). CRT gives |Ker rho_j| = prod_i gcd(t_i 2^{h_i}, t 2^j) (10.2), so 2^r |Ker rho_{g-1}| = |Ker rho_g| <= |Ker rho_h| (10.3) and |L'_n| <= 2^{-r+1} |Ker rho_h| (10.4). This gives the bound directly for r >= 3; for r = 2, Theorem 10.2 shows n is not Carmichael, so |Ker rho_h| <= |Z_n^*|/2.
The algorithm MR(n,k) runs k independent iterations; by Theorem 10.3 a composite input is accepted with probability at most 4^{-k}, while a prime input is always accepted.

Reading status: the complete proof of Theorem 10.3 was read in review. Theorem 10.4 is NOT an analysis of the number of tests: it states gamma(m,1) <= exp[-(1+o(1)) log(m) log(log(log(m)))/log(log(m))] for the probability that Algorithm RP (random prime generation with one Miller-Rabin iteration) outputs a composite, and its proof is 'Literature - see Section 10.5' (printed p. 313). The expected running time O(l^4 + k l^3) of Algorithm RP is (10.6), and the bound gamma(m,k) <= 4^{-k+1} gamma(m,1)/(1 - gamma(m,1)) is (10.7). [Corrected in review: the draft described Theorem 10.4 as 'the distribution of the number of tests performed'.]
acceptance: CN.1's acceptance condition requires probable prime and proven prime to be SEPARATE result types. Miller-Rabin yields only 'probable prime'; the AKS node yields 'proven prime'. An implementation that conflates them is unsound.
Carmichael test: n = 561 = 3 . 11 . 17 satisfies L_n = Z_n^*, so Theorem 10.1's bound does not apply to it; check that Theorem 10.3 still gives |L'_{561}| <= 140.
Check the one-sidedness explicitly: there is no bound on the probability of rejecting a prime, because that probability is zero.
Cost check: one Miller-Rabin iteration costs O(len(n)^3) while trial division by small primes costs O(len(n)) per prime, which is why the source recommends trial-division preprocessing.

nodes.title: AKS: a deterministic polynomial-time primality proof, with its exact running-time bound
nodes.statement: (Theorem 21.1) For an integer n > 1: if n is prime then (X + a)^n = X^n + a in Z_n[X] for all a in Z_n; conversely if n is composite then that identity FAILS for every a in Z_n^*. Algorithm AKS: (1) reject if n = a^b with a, b > 1; (2) find the least r > 1 with either gcd(n,r) > 1, or gcd(n,r) = 1 and the multiplicative order of [n]_r in Z_r^* greater than 4 len(n)^2; (3) accept if r = n; (4) reject if gcd(n,r) > 1; (5) for j = 1 to 2 len(n) floor(r^{1/2}) + 1, reject if (X + j)^n != X^n + j modulo X^r - 1 in Z_n[X]; (6) accept. (Theorem 21.2) For n > 1 and m >= 1 the least prime r with r not dividing n and the order of [n]_r greater than m is O(m^2 len(n)); hence the r found in step 2, which need not be prime, is O(len(n)^5). (Theorem 21.3) AKS can be implemented in time O(len(n)^{16.5}). (Theorem 21.4) A prime input is accepted. (Theorem 21.5) A composite input is rejected.
hypotheses: Theorem 21.1's converse direction needs a in Z_n^*, not merely a in Z_n; the proof uses that p^k does not divide binomial(n,p) for a prime p with n = p^k m and p not dividing m
Step 2's threshold is the multiplicative order exceeding 4 len(n)^2, and step 5's loop bound is 2 len(n) floor(r^{1/2}) + 1; both constants enter the correctness proof

Step 1's perfect-power test supplies assumption (A1) 'n is not a prime power' in the proof of Theorem 21.5 (printed p. 552). The source does not discuss whether a prime power could pass the tests of step 5 if step 1 were omitted. [Corrected in review: the draft asserted that without step 1 'the argument in step 5 can be satisfied by prime powers', which the source does not state.]
Step 3 covers the case where the search reaches r = n, which happens only for small n
The running time O(len(n)^{16.5}) is for the implementation described, using classical (not fast) arithmetic in Z_n[X]/(X^r - 1)
proofSteps: Theorem 21.1, forward: (X+a)^n = X^n + a^n + sum_{i=1}^{n-1} binomial(n,i) a^i X^{n-i}; for prime n every binomial(n,i) with 1 <= i <= n-1 is divisible by n and a^n = a by Fermat, so the identity holds in Z_n[X].

Theorem 21.1, converse: for composite n take a prime p | n with n = p^k m, p not dividing m; the numerator of binomial(n,p) = n(n-1)...(n-p+1)/p! is divisible by p^k and no higher power, the denominator by p and no higher power, so p^k does not divide binomial(n,p); with a in Z_n^* the coefficient of X^{n-p} is non-zero.

Theorem 21.2 (printed pp. 550-551): a prime r is 'bad' if r | n or r | (n^d - 1) for some d <= m, so if all primes up to x are bad then their product divides n prod_{d=1}^{m} (n^d - 1); taking logarithms gives sum_{r<=x} log r <= (log n)(1 + m(m+1)/2), and Chebyshev's lower bound sum_{r<=x} log r >= c x (Shoup Theorem 5.7) gives x = O(m^2 len(n)).

Theorem 21.3: with r = O(len(n)^5), step 5 performs O(r^{1/2} len(n)) exponentiations to the power n in Z_n[X]/(X^r - 1); each takes O(len(n)) ring operations, each of which takes O(r^2) operations in Z_n, each of which takes time O(len(n)^2).
Theorem 21.5 is the substantial direction and is proved through Lemmas 21.6-21.11, using the ring E built from Z_n[X]/(X^r-1), the sets C(alpha) and D(k), and the assumptions (A1)-(A5).
PROOF-READING BOUNDARY: Lemmas 21.6-21.11 and the assumptions (A1)-(A5) were read as statements only; the proof of Theorem 21.5 was not read in detail.
acceptance: CN.1's acceptance condition on separate result types: AKS produces a PROVEN prime, with no error probability, and this is what distinguishes it from Miller-Rabin.

Practicality check: the source states explicitly that AKS 'has no real practical significance' compared with Miller-Rabin; an implementation choosing AKS for performance reasons is misreading the source.
Check each of the five steps separately on small inputs, in particular n = 9 (rejected in step 1) and n = 2, 3 (accepted in step 3).
Check the exponent 16.5 is for the stated implementation; a faster polynomial arithmetic changes it, and the source's bound should not be quoted as intrinsic.

sources.locator: Theorem 21.1 with proof, Fig. 21.1 (Algorithm AKS), Theorem 21.2 with proof, Theorem 21.3 with proof, Theorems 21.4 and 21.5, printed pp. 548-552
sources.excerpt: Theorem 21.1. Let n > 1 be an integer. If n is prime, then for all a in Z_n, we have the following identity in the ring Z_n[X]: (X + a)^n = X^n + a. Conversely, if n is composite, then for all a in Z_n^*, the identity (21.1) does not hold. ... Theorem 21.3. Algorithm AKS can be implemented so that its running time is O(len(n)^{16.5}). ... Theorem 21.5. If the input to Algorithm AKS is composite, then the output is false.

nodes.title: Square-free decomposition, distinct-degree and equal-degree factorization, with operation counts
nodes.statement: Let F be a finite field of characteristic p with q elements and f in F[X] monic of degree l > 0. (Theorem 20.3) If gcd(f, D(f)) = f then f = g(X^p) for some g, and writing g = sum_i a_i X^i one has f = h^p with h = sum_i a_i^{p^{w-1}} X^i. (Theorem 20.4) If f = f_1^{e_1} ... f_r^{e_r} is the factorization into irreducibles then f/gcd(f, D(f)) = prod over those i with e_i not == 0 (mod p) of f_i. (Theorem 20.5) Algorithm SFD computes a square-free decomposition using O(l^2 + l (w-1) len(p)/p) operations in F. (Theorem 20.6) Distinct-degree factorization uses O(l^3 len(q)) operations in F. (Theorems 20.7, 20.8) Equal-degree splitting uses an expected O(k l^2 len(q)) operations in F, for p = 2 and for p > 2 respectively. (Theorem 20.9) The whole Cantor-Zassenhaus algorithm uses an expected O(l^3 len(q)) operations in F, and this bound is tight (attained when the input is irreducible). (Theorem 20.10) Berlekamp's Algorithm B1 uses O(l^3 + l^2 len(q)) operations in F.
hypotheses: All counts are in OPERATIONS IN F, not bit operations; converting requires multiplying by the cost of an F-operation, which is where the RAM/bit model of CN.0 enters
q = p^w; the square-free decomposition cost has a term depending on w and p separately because of the p-th power extraction in Theorem 20.3

Equal-degree splitting is PROBABILISTIC: the bounds in Theorems 20.7 and 20.8 are expected values, and the failure probability per pair of irreducible factors is 1/2 for p = 2 and at most 5/9 for p > 2
Cantor-Zassenhaus as analysed assumes a square-free input; SFD is used as preprocessing and the bound of Theorem 20.9 survives that preprocessing

Berlekamp's Algorithm B1 (Theorem 20.10) only computes a basis of the Berlekamp subalgebra B = {alpha : alpha^q = alpha} of F[X]/(f), by Gaussian elimination on an l x l matrix over F; it does not factor f. Stage 2 of Berlekamp's algorithm, which splits f using that basis, is a PROBABILISTIC procedure (success probability at least 1/2 for p = 2 and 4/9 for p > 2 per split, printed pp. 540-541). [Corrected in review: the draft presented B1 as the deterministic factoring alternative.]

PLACEMENT NOTE (added in review): the atlas description of FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums:FF.3 is 'Prove finite-field polynomial factorization, Hensel interfaces and certified point-counting algorithms', and CN.1 requires FF.3. The mathematics of this node, Shoup Chapter 20, is therefore FF.3's declared scope, while CN.1's role is to implement factorization 'using checked factors and irreducibility proofs'. The EXT-08 FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums packet records Chapter 20 as unread under FF.3. The orchestrator should decide whether to move this node under FF.3 and keep a CN.1 consumer node, or leave it here with an FF.3 -> CN.1 edge.
proofSteps: Theorem 20.3: gcd(f, D(f)) = f forces D(f) = 0 since deg D(f) < deg f; writing f = sum_i c_i X^i, D(f) = sum_i i c_i X^{i-1} = 0 forces c_i = 0 unless p | i, so f = g(X^p); the p-th root is extracted coefficientwise using the Frobenius, giving the exponent p^{w-1}.
Theorem 20.4 is a direct consequence of Theorem 20.3 together with the multiplicity bookkeeping for the derivative.

Theorem 20.5 is proved by tracking, at the beginning of the j-th inner iteration, that g = prod_{i in S_{>=j}} f_i and f = prod_{i in S_{>=j}} f_i^{e_i - j + 1} prod_{i in S'} f_i^{e_i}, where S is the set of i with e_i not divisible by p and S' its complement.
Theorem 20.6: the main loop runs at most l times, each iteration performing a q-th powering at O(l^2 len(q)) operations plus gcd and division at O(l^2), giving O(l^3 len(q)).

Theorems 20.7-20.9 (printed pp. 532-537). A quick bound gives expected O(l^3 len(q)) for EDF. For p = 2, Theorem 20.7 first shows E[L] = O(len(r)) for the number L of loop iterations, by a union bound over pairs (i,j) with P[L_ij >= n] = 2^{-(n-1)} (a pair not yet separated is separated in the next iteration with probability 1/2). The sharper O(k l^2 len(q)) then comes from S = sum_{i,j} L_ij with E[S] = 2r(r-1) + O(r len(r)) = O(r^2). Theorem 20.8 (p > 2) is left as an exercise with failure probability at most 5/9 per pair. Theorem 20.9 combines DDF (Theorem 20.6) with the quick EDF bound summed over the degree classes. [Corrected in review: the draft described a 'coupling argument'.]
Reading status: the proof of Theorem 20.7 was read in review. Theorem 20.8's proof is left as an exercise in the source, and Section 20.6 (deterministic factorization algorithms) was not read.
acceptance: CN.1's acceptance condition requires that a factorization output multiply back to the input. Check this after each of the three phases separately (square-free, distinct-degree, equal-degree), since each phase has its own invariant.
Check the p | e_i case in Theorem 20.4: those factors are invisible to f/gcd(f,D(f)) and are recovered only via the p-th root of Theorem 20.3.

Check the randomness model: Theorems 20.7 and 20.8 bound an EXPECTED cost, so no worst-case deterministic bound can be quoted from them. Berlekamp's Algorithm B1 is deterministic, but it only computes a basis of the Berlekamp subalgebra, and Berlekamp's splitting stage is probabilistic; deterministic factorization is Section 20.6, which was not read. [Corrected in review.]
Check the tightness remark for Theorem 20.9: an irreducible input really does cost O(l^3 len(q)) operations.

This bound is tight, since in the worst case, when the input is irreducible, the algorithm really does do this much work.

The detailed probabilistic analysis behind Theorems 20.7 and 20.8 was not read, and Theorem 20.8's proof is left as an exercise in the source.
Deterministic factorization algorithms (Shoup section 20.6) not read.
Theorem 21.2's proof imports Chebyshev's lower bound (Shoup Theorem 5.7, Chapter 5), not read.
Placement: Shoup Chapter 20 (finite-field polynomial factorization) is FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums:FF.3's declared scope; see the gap on placement.

Integral bases, orders, ideal decomposition, unit and class groups, local expansions: no source read. Shoup does not treat number fields, so the SHOUP half of this stage's source route cannot supply CN.2 at all; a separate source (for example Cohen's 'A Course in Computational Algebraic Number Theory', not freely available) is required.
Modular symbols, Hecke matrices, q-expansions, point counts, isogenies, Sturm bounds: no source read. Shoup covers none of this.

Interval/ball arithmetic, precision propagation, certified roots, L-value approximation: no source read. Shoup does not treat validated numerics. Note that CN.4 requires AnalyticNumberTheory:AN.4, which IS partially decomposed in the EXT-08 AnalyticNumberTheory packet (Hecke L-functions and their functional equations); the numerical-evaluation half has no source.
Certificate schemas, dataset provenance, benchmark reporting: no source read; this is a methodology stage rather than a mathematical one.

gaps.title: Integer factorization has no read source anywhere in EXT-08
gaps.detail: Verified: polynomial factorization over finite fields (Shoup Chapter 20) with full operation counts, and both primality routes (Miller-Rabin and AKS). Not verified: any integer factoring algorithm. Shoup Chapter 15 ('Subexponential-time discrete logarithms and factoring', printed pp. 399-418) covers the quadratic-sieve-style method and was located in the table of contents but not read; the number field sieve is not in Shoup at all. Next source action: read Shoup Chapter 15 (no new acquisition needed) and record the smoothness hypotheses and the heuristic versus proved status of the running times -- Shoup is careful about which factoring running times are heuristic.

gaps.title: Primality certificates versus primality tests
gaps.detail: CN.1 asks for 'primality certificates and source-scoped deterministic/probabilistic tests'. What was read supplies TESTS: Miller-Rabin (probabilistic, one-sided) and AKS (deterministic). Neither produces a short independently checkable certificate: AKS's 'proof' is the whole execution trace. Verified: the exact statements and the running-time bound. Not verified: any certificate scheme. Next source action: select a source for Pratt certificates (elementary, from Lucas's converse of Fermat) and, if elliptic-curve certificates are wanted, an ECPP reference; neither is in Shoup.

gaps.title: CN.0's carrier and conversion requirements are unmet
gaps.detail: CN.0 asks for exact representations of integers, rationals, algebraic numbers, finite fields, ideals, lattices and p-adic approximations, with conversions carrying equality/embedding proofs, and for canonical mathematical carriers separated from computable presentations. Verified: only the RAM model and the bit-complexity convention. Shoup does supply finite-field presentations (Chapter 19, read for the FF packet: E = F[X]/(f) with the isomorphism of Theorem 19.14), but nothing about ideals, lattices or p-adic approximations, and nothing about carrier/presentation separation. Next source action: this stage's requirements are partly a formalization-design question rather than a source question; the mathematical half needs Shoup Chapters 16-17 plus a lattice source.

gaps.title: Shoup cannot supply CN.2, CN.3 or CN.4
gaps.detail: Checked against the table of contents, printed pp. v-ix: the book's 21 chapters cover integers, congruences, computing with large integers, Euclid's algorithm, the distribution of primes, abelian groups, rings, probability, probabilistic algorithms, primality testing, discrete logarithms, quadratic reciprocity, modules and vector spaces, matrices, subexponential algorithms, more rings, polynomial arithmetic, linearly generated sequences, finite fields, algorithms for finite fields, and deterministic primality testing. There is no number-field, modular-forms or validated-numerics material. CN.2-CN.4 therefore need sources outside this roadmap's declared route (SHOUP, LOCAL). Recorded so that the route is not treated as adequate.

gaps.title: Finite-field polynomial factorization is FF.3's declared scope but is decomposed under CN.1
gaps.detail: Added in review (REVIEW-EXT-08-EXT-16). data/atlas.json assigns 'Prove finite-field polynomial factorization, Hensel interfaces and certified point-counting algorithms' to FiniteFieldsAndCharacterSums:FF.3, and CN.1 requires FF.3. The protocol prefers one supplier to a duplicate construction. Decision needed: move the node to FF.3 and keep in CN.1 only the checked-factor implementation contract, or record CN.1 as the owner and drop the claim from FF.3's scope.

review.notes: All 4 nodes and 3 draft links were checked against Shoup, Version 2, re-fetched (SHA-256 8e1abc54... matches; printed page = PDF page - 18). Corrections: (1) The RAM model node omitted the source's unit-cost-per-instruction rule and the polynomial magnitude restriction on stored numbers, and wrongly said unit-cost steps and bit operations differ by an unbounded factor in this model. (2) Theorem 10.4 was misdescribed as a distribution of the number of tests; it is a literature-cited bound on gamma(m,1). The definition of L'_n missed the alpha^t = 1 case; Theorem 10.2 is completed; the three-case proof of Theorem 10.3 was read and recorded. (3) The claim that prime powers can pass step 5 of AKS without step 1 is not in the source; step 1 supplies assumption (A1). Theorem 21.2's use of Chebyshev's bound is named. (4) Berlekamp's B1 was presented as a deterministic factoring alternative, but it only computes a basis of the Berlekamp subalgebra and the splitting stage is probabilistic; the EDF analysis is a union bound over pairs, not a coupling argument. (5) The link Miller-Rabin -> AKS was REMOVED: the draft itself said it is not a mathematical dependency, and the result-type contract is already recorded in both nodes' acceptance items. (6) The FF.0 census -> factorization link reason wrongly called itself the content of the atlas edge FF.3 -> CN.1. Placement finding: finite-field polynomial factorization is FF.3's declared atlas scope; a gap and a node placement note were added for the orchestrator. parentStageIds CN.0 and CN.1 exist and belong to ComputationalNumberTheory; all six coverage ids exist. Packet status stays partial.
